course.title: Concurrency you can replay: forced interleavings
course.description: Races proven with latches and a pausing map instead of sleeps: atomic map updates, create-once caches, graceful executor shutdown, a fail-fast bulkhead, deadlines that cancel, and a worker that honours interruption (JDK 17).

unit.title: A ConcurrentHashMap counter that loses no update
One client per tenant, even when two requests race
Shut an executor down: grace, then force
A bulkhead: at most N calls in flight, the rest rejected
Wait for a result with a deadline, and cancel what is late
A queue worker that stops when it is interrupted

javadrills/13-forced-interleavings/01-lo.instructions:
**Skills:** ConcurrentHashMap · atomic updates · deterministic tests  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Page views are counted in a `ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer>`. It is a concurrent map, so the counts are right, aren't they? Prove it with a test that fails every time, not one time in a thousand."

**Why it matters.** Every single call on a `ConcurrentHashMap` is thread-safe, but `get` followed by `put` is two calls: another thread can write between them and its update is overwritten. `merge` and `compute` do the read and the write as one atomic step per key. A race is tested deterministically by forcing the bad interleaving: the given `PausingMap` stops thread `A` right after its `get` read the value, lets the test thread increment, then lets `A` finish.

**Your task.** Implement `static void increment(ConcurrentMap<String, Integer> counts, String key)`:
- add 1 to the key's count, starting from 1 for a key that is not there
- correct under any interleaving of calls from different threads
- a `null` key is refused with `NullPointerException` (the map does that for you)

**Worked example.** `A` reads `null` for `"home"` and pauses; the test thread increments `"home"` to 1; `A` resumes. A get-then-put leaves 1, the right answer is 2.
hints: Two calls on a thread-safe map are not one thread-safe operation. Something else can happen between them.
Use the single map operation that combines the new value with whatever is already stored, so reading and writing happen as one step for that key.
Merge one into the key with integer addition as the combining function, or compute the new value from the old one in a single call.

javadrills/13-forced-interleavings/02-cr.instructions:
**Skills:** ConcurrentHashMap · lazy initialisation · deterministic tests  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Each tenant gets one HTTP client with its own connection pool, created on first use. In production we sometimes see two pools for one tenant, and one of them is never closed."

**Why it matters.** `if (cache.get(t) == null) cache.put(t, create(t))` lets two threads both see `null` and both create. `putIfAbsent` keeps only one of the two in the map, but the second object was still built (and here, leaked). `computeIfAbsent` runs the factory at most once per key while it holds that key's bin, and records nothing when the factory throws.

**Your task.** Implement `static Client clientFor(ConcurrentMap<String, Client> cache, String tenant, Function<String, Client> factory)`:
- return the tenant's client, calling `factory` only when there is none yet
- under any interleaving, `factory` runs once per tenant and every caller gets the same instance
- a factory that throws caches nothing; the exception reaches the caller and the next call tries again
- the factory must not touch `cache` itself (a `ConcurrentHashMap` may refuse that)

**Worked example.** Thread `A` looks up `acme`, sees nothing and pauses; the test thread asks for `acme` too. The factory must run once, and both callers hold the same client.
hints: Looking up and then storing is two steps, and another request can arrive between them. Building first and then storing has the same gap.
One map operation takes the key and a function, runs the function only when the key is missing and stores the result as part of the same step.
Hand the tenant and the factory to the map operation that computes a value only if the key is absent, and hand back what it gives you.

javadrills/13-forced-interleavings/03-sh.instructions:
**Skills:** ExecutorService · interruption · graceful shutdown  
**Level:** ★★★

**Interview prompt.** "On deploy the old instance hangs for minutes, and sometimes it exits with half the queued emails unsent and no log line saying so. Write the shutdown hook."

**Why it matters.** `shutdown()` stops new work and lets queued tasks run; `awaitTermination` waits a bounded time; only `shutdownNow()` interrupts the running tasks, and it hands back the tasks that never started, so you can log or re-queue them. A caller that is itself interrupted must not swallow that: it finishes the shutdown and sets its interrupt flag again so its own caller sees it.

**Your task.** Implement `static int shutdownGracefully(ExecutorService pool, long graceMs)`:
- stop accepting new tasks and let running and queued tasks finish, waiting up to `graceMs`
- if they all finished: return 0
- otherwise interrupt what is running, wait up to `graceMs` again for it to stop, and return how many queued tasks never started
- if the calling thread is interrupted while waiting: interrupt the pool's tasks, set the caller's interrupt flag again, and return how many queued tasks never started

**Worked example.** A one-thread pool runs a task that blocks until interrupted, with two more queued. `shutdownGracefully(pool, 50)` waits 50 ms, interrupts the stuck task and returns 2.
hints: There are two ways to stop a pool. One lets work finish, the other interrupts it and tells you what never ran, and you need both, in a fixed order.

Stop new work and wait the grace period. If the pool is still busy, interrupt it and count the queued tasks it hands back. If your own wait is interrupted, do the same and put the interrupt flag back.

Shut down, await termination for the grace period, and only if that fails shut down now, await again and report the size of the list you got. In the interrupted branch shut down now and re-interrupt the current thread.

javadrills/13-forced-interleavings/04-a-.instructions:
**Skills:** Semaphore · bulkheads · deterministic tests  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "When the recommendations service slows down, every request thread ends up waiting on it and checkout stops too. Cap the concurrent calls and fail fast beyond the cap."

**Why it matters.** A bulkhead gives one dependency a fixed number of permits. A call takes a permit or is rejected at once, so a slow dependency can hold at most N threads. The permit must come back on every exit, including an exception, or the bulkhead leaks until nothing gets through. Blocking for a permit instead of rejecting is the queue you were trying to avoid.

**Your task.** Complete `Bulkhead(int permits)`:
- `<T> T call(Callable<T> work) throws Exception`: if no permit is free right now, throw `Rejected` without running `work`; otherwise run it and return its result
- the permit is released on every exit, also when `work` throws (its exception reaches the caller unchanged)
- `int inFlight()`: how many calls hold a permit now

**Worked example.** With 2 permits and two calls blocked inside `work`, a third call is rejected at once; when one of the two returns, the next call runs.
hints: Fail fast means you never wait for capacity. And every permit taken must come back however the call ends.
Take a permit with the semaphore method that answers at once, reject when it says no, and run the work inside a block that always hands the permit back.
Try to acquire without blocking, throw the rejection when that fails, call the work in a try block whose finally releases, and count in-flight calls from the permits still available.

javadrills/13-forced-interleavings/05-a-.instructions:
**Skills:** Future · timeouts · cancellation  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "The price lookup has a 200 ms budget. After the timeout we show a cached price, but CPU stays high: the slow lookups keep running in the pool."

**Why it matters.** `future.get(timeout, unit)` gives up WAITING; it does not stop the task. Only `future.cancel(true)` interrupts it, and only a task that responds to interruption actually stops. A failure inside the task arrives wrapped in `ExecutionException`, which callers should not have to unwrap.

**Your task.** Implement `static <T> T withDeadline(ExecutorService pool, Callable<T> work, long timeoutMs, T fallback)`:
- submit `work` and wait at most `timeoutMs` for its result
- late: cancel it with interruption and return `fallback`
- it failed: rethrow its exception if it is a `RuntimeException`, otherwise wrap it in `IllegalStateException` (with the original as the cause)
- the caller is interrupted while waiting: cancel the task, set the interrupt flag again, return `fallback`

**Worked example.** A lookup that blocks for ever with `timeoutMs = 50` returns the fallback after about 50 ms, and the lookup sees an interrupt.
hints: Giving up on a result and stopping the work that computes it are two different calls.
Wait with a timeout, and when you stop waiting for any reason other than success, cancel the task with interruption. Unwrap a failure so the caller sees the task's own exception.
Get the future with the timeout, cancel with interruption and fall back on a timeout, rethrow a runtime cause or wrap a checked one, and on interruption cancel, re-interrupt and fall back.

javadrills/13-forced-interleavings/06-a-.instructions:
**Skills:** interruption · BlockingQueue · worker loops  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Our email worker survives `shutdownNow()`: the pool never terminates and the deploy waits for its timeout. The loop catches `InterruptedException` and carries on."

**Why it matters.** Interruption is how Java asks a thread to stop. A blocking call such as `queue.take()` answers it by throwing `InterruptedException` and clearing the flag. A loop that catches it and continues turns "please stop" into "ignore me". The loop should leave, and set the flag again for whatever runs after it on that thread.

**Your task.** Implement `static void drain(BlockingQueue<String> queue, Consumer<String> send)`, a worker loop:
- take items one by one and pass each to `send`, in order, until the thread is interrupted
- interrupted while waiting for an item: leave the loop and set the interrupt flag again
- an item already taken is sent before the loop looks at the flag again
- a `send` that throws stops the worker with that exception (no item is skipped silently)

**Worked example.** Items `a`, `b` are sent, the worker blocks on an empty queue, `interrupt()` arrives: `drain` returns with the flag set, having sent `[a, b]`.
hints: The blocking call already tells you when someone wants the thread to stop. The question is what the loop does with that.

Keep taking and sending while the thread is not interrupted, and put the whole loop inside the try, so the interrupted exception ends it instead of starting the next round. Set the flag again on the way out.
Wrap a while loop on the interrupt status around take and send in a try block, and in the catch for the interrupted exception re-interrupt the current thread and fall out.
